subject: 재현과 모방 — 회화가 무엇을 어떻게 지시하는가
title: What a painting refers to
content: The oldest theory of pictorial art holds that a painting succeeds insofar as it resembles what it depicts, and this criterion governed criticism for centuries because resemblance seems measurable in a way that expression does not. Yet the standard collapses when it is examined closely. A portrait resembles its sitter far less than a photograph does, and a photograph less than a mirror, and nobody has ever called mirrors the summit of representational art. Resemblance is also symmetrical, whereas depiction is not, since a landscape resembles the canvas exactly as much as the canvas resembles it while depicting nothing at all. The difficulty deepens once we notice that resemblance always holds in some respect. Everything is like everything else in indefinitely many ways, so the criterion says nothing until we specify which respects count, and that specification was precisely what a theory of depiction was supposed to supply. Aesthetics therefore replaced resemblance with convention, treating pictures as symbols rather than mirrors. On this account a canvas refers to its subject because a community has established the practice of taking it so, much as a word refers without sounding like its object. This explains why unfamiliar pictorial systems look illegible to viewers trained elsewhere, and why perspective, once thought to record vision faithfully, is now understood as a learned notation. Realism becomes a historical achievement rather than a natural baseline, and artistic value must be argued on other grounds.

subject: 음악 청취의 역사성 — 침묵하는 청중은 언제 생겼나
title: When audiences learned to sit in silence
content: Silence in the concert hall feels like an obvious mark of respect for the music, and yet this arrangement is comparatively recent. Through much of the eighteenth century listeners conversed, ate, arrived late, and applauded between movements, and performers expected as much. The transformation into a quiet and immobile public happened gradually, and it accompanied changes that had little to do with the art itself. Halls grew larger and darker, tickets were sold to strangers rather than distributed within a court, and the printed programme appeared to tell newcomers what they were hearing. Each development encouraged a particular posture, and together they produced the modern audience. What deserves attention is how thoroughly the arrangement came to seem natural, since a cough is now experienced as an intrusion and a phone as a violation, which shows that the convention carries moral weight rather than mere etiquette. Cultural historians therefore treat attention itself as an artifact with a history, shaped by architecture, commerce, and the ambitions of composers who wanted their forms grasped whole. This has consequences for how other listening practices are judged. If concentrated silence is a convention rather than the natural response to serious music, then background listening is not obviously a degradation, and the traditions in which music accompanies work or worship are not deficient concerts. They are different arrangements, each making some features of the art audible and others inaudible.

subject: 진품과 위작 — 감상은 무엇을 보고 있는가
title: The forgery and the eye
content: A forgery may be indistinguishable from an original under any examination the eye can perform, and yet its exposure transforms our estimation of it completely. This reaction puzzles aesthetics, because if the visible properties are identical then the aesthetic experience ought to be identical as well. Something other than appearance is evidently doing the work, and two explanations compete. The first locates the difference in history rather than surface. An original stands in a particular causal relation to its maker, and that relation is part of what we value, much as a letter from a friend differs from a perfect facsimile despite identical wording. On this account authenticity is a fact about origin rather than a perceptible quality, and our response tracks the fact. The second explanation is less metaphysical, since knowing that a work is a forgery changes what we look for and therefore changes what we see. A connoisseur who learns of the deception begins to notice hesitations in the brushwork that previously read as confidence. Neither account is complete on its own. The historical one cannot explain why forgeries sometimes survive expert scrutiny for decades, and the perceptual one cannot explain why our estimation falls even when no new visual difference is ever found. What both establish is that aesthetic judgment reaches beyond the surface presented to the eye, and that a document in an archive can alter a painting which has not changed physically at all.

subject: 번역에서 옮겨지지 않는 것
title: What translation cannot carry
content: Every literary translator meets passages that appear to resist transfer entirely, among them a pun whose two senses have no common equivalent, a form of address encoding a social relation the target language does not mark, and a rhythm inseparable from the sounds that carry it. The traditional response treats these as losses to be minimized, so that the translator's task becomes recovering as much as circumstances permit. A different tradition regards them as the most instructive part of the work. On that view the untranslatable is not a defect in the target language but evidence about the source, since the resistance reveals what a language obliges its speakers to specify. A tongue that distinguishes several degrees of formality compels a choice that another leaves open, and the translator who must select among options discovers a structure that native readers never notice. Difficulty therefore becomes a method of cultural description rather than an obstacle to it. This reframing changes the standard by which a translation is judged. If fidelity means producing the same effect, then departing from the words is legitimate, and a pun may be replaced by a different pun. If fidelity means preserving the strangeness, then the translation should retain what the target language finds awkward, letting readers feel the shape of a system unlike their own. The two ideals cannot both be satisfied, and choosing between them is an interpretive judgment about what readers are owed.

subject: 즉흥연주 — 준비의 산물로서의 자유
title: Improvisation as the fruit of preparation
content: Listeners often describe improvisation as playing without any plan, as though the performer made up each phrase at the moment of sounding it. Musicians who improvise tell a different story, and they speak of a stock of figures built up over years, of runs drilled until the hand finds them without thought, and of chord shapes so well learned that attention can rest on the arc of a solo rather than on the fingers. Freedom, on their account, is not the opposite of practice but its fruit, since only long practice makes fast choice possible. This point matters because the common picture hands improvisation to instinct and writing to labour, and that split shapes how whole traditions are ranked. Music passed on by ear rather than by score has often been called natural, and the word, though meant as praise, denies those players the credit given to written music for craft and thought. What sounds easy is thus mistaken for what took no work. Studies of skill back the players rather than the listeners, since good improvisers lean on stored patterns much as chess masters do when they read a board, and their ease comes from recall rather than from invention. The freedom an audience hears is real, and yet it works inside a frame that rules out most moves in advance. Seeing this puts the feat where players have always put it, and it strips away the faint scorn that follows whenever skill is renamed instinct.

subject: 사진이 회화에 남긴 문제
title: The problem photography left for painting
content: When photography became widely available, painters lost a function they had performed for centuries, since a likeness could now be obtained faster, cheaper, and with an accuracy no hand could match. Art history often tells the story as a liberation, with painting freed to pursue what only painting could do, and the movements that followed are read as the consequence. That account is tidy, and the evidence complicates it in useful ways. Portrait painters did not vanish, and many of them used photographs as aids while continuing to sell what the camera could not supply, namely a considered interpretation of a sitter rather than a record of one instant. Meanwhile photographers spent decades arguing that their medium was an art rather than a mechanical trace, and they made that case by imitating painting, softening focus and arranging subjects in the compositions painters had established. Each medium therefore borrowed the other's authority while claiming to be different in kind. What the episode illustrates is that a new technology does not simply take over a function and leave the rest untouched. It changes what the older practice is understood to be about, and the change runs in both directions. Painting became more explicitly interpretive because a mechanical alternative existed, and photography acquired aesthetic ambitions because it needed an argument against being merely mechanical.

subject: 서사의 시간 — 이야기와 사건의 순서
title: Story time and the order of telling
content: A narrative arranges events in an order, and that order need not match the sequence in which the events occurred. Literary theory marks the difference by separating the story, which is what happened, from the telling, which is how it reaches us, and the gap between them is where much of a narrative's effect is produced. A tale that opens at its end asks a different question of the reader than one that begins at the beginning. Several devices exploit this gap systematically. Withholding an event that has already occurred creates suspense about the past rather than the future, and revealing an outcome early shifts attention from what will happen to how it came about. Repetition of a single event from different vantage points, common in modern fiction, denies the reader any settled account and makes the discrepancy itself the subject. None of these effects would be available if telling simply mirrored occurrence. What follows is that the order of narration carries meaning independently of the events narrated. Two texts reporting identical happenings can differ entirely in what they assert, because emphasis, causal suggestion, and moral weight are conveyed by arrangement. Critics therefore treat the sequence of telling as evidence about a work's argument rather than as a neutral container for its content, and the same principle applies to history and journalism as much as to fiction.

subject: 원근법은 발견인가 약속인가
title: Perspective as discovery or as agreement
content: Linear perspective is often presented as a discovery, a set of rules by which painters finally learned to record space as the eye actually receives it. That description has an obvious appeal, since pictures built on those rules do look convincing to viewers raised among them. Yet several considerations suggest that perspective is better understood as a convention which became familiar rather than as a fact about vision. The eye moves constantly and takes in a curved field, whereas perspective assumes a single fixed viewpoint and a flat plane, so the system matches an idealization rather than an experience. Cultures that developed sophisticated pictorial traditions without it did not fail at a task they attempted; they were solving different problems, such as showing what an object is rather than how it appears from one place. Viewers unfamiliar with the convention have been observed to read perspectival pictures incorrectly, which would be strange if the system merely recorded seeing. What makes the question more than academic is what follows for judgment. If perspective is a discovery, then traditions lacking it are less advanced, and the history of art becomes a story of progress toward accuracy. If it is a convention, then those traditions made different choices about what a picture is for, and the appearance of naturalness in our own is an artifact of long exposure rather than evidence of correctness.

subject: 가면과 배우 — 연기의 인류학
title: Masks and the performer who wears them
content: Masked performance appears in many cultural traditions, and it raises a question that ordinary acting does not, because a mask fixes the face while the body beneath it continues to move. Modern audiences trained on naturalistic performance often assume the mask is a limitation the performer works around, yet practitioners describe the opposite relationship, treating the fixed face as the source of what they can express. This reversal is worth examining, since it exposes assumptions about where expression is located. A mask gives the performer a single external image, so meaning must be produced by angle, rhythm, and the relation of the body to that unchanging face. Small movements register enormously against a constant, and audiences report reading emotion into masks that have not moved at all. In traditions where the mask represents a being other than the performer, the fixity is essential rather than incidental, because the figure must not appear to be improvising a personality. What the practice reveals about performance generally is that expression depends on contrast rather than on the face alone. An unmasked actor also works against a constant, namely the audience's expectation of how a person in that situation would behave, and departures from it carry the meaning. The mask makes this structure visible by removing the resource that usually conceals it.

subject: 초상화가 기록한 권력
title: Power recorded in the portrait
content: A portrait appears to record a face, and yet the surviving portraits of any period record a great deal more, since being painted at all required resources and a reason. Who was represented, in what setting, and holding which objects were decisions made before the sitting began, and cultural historians read those decisions as evidence about the society that produced them. The face is often the least informative element. Attributes carried the argument. A book indicated learning, a map indicated reach, and a particular fabric indicated an income that sumptuary rules may have restricted to certain ranks. Because viewers of the period read these signs fluently, the painter could make a claim without stating it, and the claim was frequently about a position the sitter wished to be granted rather than one securely held. Portraits commissioned during a rise in fortune are accordingly more assertive than those commissioned by families long established. What complicates the reading is that these conventions changed, so a pose that asserted authority in one century looked stiff or comic in the next, and later viewers who miss the shift misjudge the tone entirely. Cultural historians therefore date the conventions before interpreting the picture, treating the portrait as a document produced under rules that must be reconstructed rather than as a window onto a person.

subject: 악보가 연주에 남긴 여백
title: What notation leaves to the performer
content: A musical score looks like a complete set of instructions, and yet no score determines a performance, since notation records pitch and duration with precision while leaving much else unspecified. How loud a passage should be, how much a tempo may bend, and what quality of tone suits a phrase are questions that performers answer rather than read. This gap is not a defect of the system but a feature of what notation was built to do. Historical evidence shows the gap widening and narrowing over time. Earlier scores assumed a shared performing tradition and recorded only what could not be assumed, so a modern player who follows them literally produces something the composer never intended. Later composers, writing for performers they would never meet, filled in more and more, and some twentieth-century scores specify details that once belonged entirely to practice. Each approach transfers authority between the page and the player, and neither eliminates the transfer. What follows is that the identity of a musical work cannot lie in the score alone. Two performances differing in everything the notation omits are still performances of the same piece, which means the work includes a range of realizations rather than a single correct one. Judging performances therefore requires standards that the score cannot supply, and those standards come from a tradition that is transmitted by hearing rather than by reading.

subject: 도자기 문양의 전파
title: How ceramic patterns travelled
content: Decorated pottery survives where textiles and wood do not, and its patterns therefore serve as one of the best records we have of contact between cultural traditions. When a motif appears far from where it originated, something moved, and the archaeological task is to determine what. The vessel itself may have travelled, or a potter may have migrated, or a local maker may have copied a piece brought by someone else, and each possibility implies a different kind of connection. The manner of copying supplies the evidence. A potter who understood the original tradition reproduces not only the motif but the sequence of strokes that produce it, whereas one working from a finished object alone arrives at a similar appearance by a different route, and the difference shows under close examination. Where the pattern is reproduced but the clay and firing are local, the object was made on the spot by someone who had seen the design without learning the craft behind it. What such analysis yields is a map of cultural contact that written sources rarely record, since pots moved along routes used by people whose transactions nobody wrote down. Historians accordingly treat decorated ceramics as testimony about ordinary exchange rather than as evidence of elite diplomacy, and the patterns become a record of who actually met whom.
